newsitem.title: UK: Mexico peso fall haunts investors but no disaster.
newsitem.headline: Mexico peso fall haunts investors but no disaster.

text.p: Mexico's tumbling currency has summoned up the ghost of the peso crisis nearly two years ago which brought many emerging markets close to the abyss, but analysts on Thursday said this time it is less hair-raising.
Some feel that a bit more of a drop in the peso would even help Mexico's painful economic recovery and that it is not a repeat of the near catastrophe the peso devaluation brought at the end of 1994.
"There is a risk of a rerun of history but I don't think that is what is happening yet," said ABN-AMRO chief economist for Latin America Ian Campbell.
Mexico's peso has dropped some four percent in the past week to 7.80 to the dollar in what finance ministry officials insist is normal volatility that should soon die down.
Analysts said one of the triggers was disappointment in the market over the government's retreat earlier this month on plans to privatise state-owned petrochemical plants.

It was for many a disturbing sign that the government was not as committed to the reforms it must implement to keep the economy on its path towards recovery after near collapse at the end of 1994 when it devalued the peso.
At that time however, Mexico was battling a large current account deficit. Now it has a healthy surplus, with exports continuing to rise.
"It sends quite a bad signal for the future," Janet Krengel, senior economist at IBCA ratings agency, said of the backsliding on petrochemical sales.
But, as with a number of analysts, she was not worried by the peso's decline except for the speed.
"I'd expect and hope for a gentle weakening to maintain (export) competition and avoid speculative attacks," she said.
Joe MacHatton, Latin American strategist at Kleinwort Benson, hoped to see a peso worth closer to nine to the dollar in six months.

It won't be until 1998 that the economic is back to its level before the 1994 peso crisis, he said, urging investors to go underweight in Mexican shares in view of disappointing prospects for corporate earnings.
Others, however, felt the peso's current level was fine and some expect it to bounce back.
"(The peso) is not a big issue. It is something that will blow over...I don't see any fundamental problems in Mexico at all," added ANZ analyst Jerome Booth.
ABN-Amro's Campbell said that as the economic recovery does get underway so there was a need to see the peso value slip.
"In the long-term, Mexico needs export-led growth, therefore a strong peso would be worrying. But that time has not come," he said.
